what: NOV makes the equipment that drills oil and gas wells. Its products include drilling rigs and their components, drill pipe, downhole tools, pumps, pressure control equipment and the systems used on offshore rigs and in fibreglass pipe and composite applications.
customers: Drilling contractors who own rigs, oilfield service companies, and national and international oil companies, across land and offshore operations worldwide.
money: Drill pipe, downhole tools, pumps, pressure pumping equipment and aftermarket parts.
Rig equipment, offshore systems, process technologies and composite pipe.
moat: NOV’s equipment is on a very large share of the world’s rigs, and that installed base generates spare parts and service revenue for decades regardless of whether anyone is building new rigs. Rig equipment is also heavily engineered and certified, so a drilling contractor does not switch supplier casually. The aftermarket is the steady part of a famously unsteady industry.
risks: Net income of $143.0M on $8.7B of revenue is a 1.6% margin, and the price/earnings ratio of about 40 reflects depressed earnings rather than a growth premium.
Revenue has flattened at about $8.7B to $8.9B after recovering from the 2021 trough, so the cyclical upswing appears to have stalled.
Very few new rigs are being built, which is the structural problem: NOV’s largest historical product has a shrinking market.
Offshore and international activity drives much of the remaining demand, and both depend on oil company capital budgets.
Twenty analysts average a $22.15 target, about 35% above the current price.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 0.68 times sales and 8.2 times EV/EBITDA, undemanding even for an oilfield equipment maker.
Cash of $1.6B against $2.1B of debt is a far stronger balance sheet than the company carried in previous cycles.
The aftermarket and spare parts business is tied to rigs operating rather than rigs being built, which is a much steadier demand pattern.
Offshore drilling has begun recovering after a decade of underinvestment, and NOV’s offshore equipment franchise is substantial.
watch: The split between new equipment orders and aftermarket revenue. New rig building is structurally diminished; the aftermarket on the existing fleet is what this company is actually worth.
view: NOV is a reminder that a dominant position in a shrinking market is a complicated asset. It makes a very large share of the world’s drilling equipment, and for most of its history that meant selling rigs and rig components during building cycles. Those cycles have essentially ended: almost nobody is ordering new drilling rigs, because the last building boom left the industry with more than it needed and bankrupted several of its customers. The largest historical product line has a structurally smaller market and is not coming back.

What remains is better than the share price suggests. NOV’s equipment is installed across the global fleet, and that installed base needs drill pipe, downhole tools, spare parts and service for as long as the rigs operate. Aftermarket demand follows rigs working rather than rigs being built, which is a far steadier pattern and a far better business. The question for anyone buying this is what proportion of revenue comes from that, because the aftermarket deserves a much higher multiple than the equipment line.

On the numbers, a price/earnings ratio of 40 on a 1.6% net margin is the market correctly ignoring depressed earnings — nobody is paying a growth premium here. At 0.68 times sales and 8.2 times EV/EBITDA you are paying roughly book-value economics for a company with $1.6 billion of cash against $2.1 billion of debt, which is a much stronger balance sheet than NOV carried into previous downturns. That matters: the way oilfield equipment companies die is leverage meeting a cycle.

The upside case rests on offshore, which has begun recovering after a decade of underinvestment and where NOV’s franchise is genuinely strong. The twenty analysts at $22.15 are modelling that recovery. The risk is that it recovers more slowly than hoped while land drilling stays flat, leaving a cheap company that stays cheap for years. This is a value situation rather than a growth one, and the honest holding period is measured in years, not quarters. Watch the aftermarket share of revenue; it is the part that justifies owning this at all.
bull: Offshore activity keeps recovering, the aftermarket on a vast installed fleet provides a steady base, and a 0.68 times sales multiple on a net-cash-adjusted balance sheet re-rates.
bear: New rig building never returns, land activity stays flat, and a 1.6% margin business with no growth simply stays cheap for years.
